title: A multi-wavelength view of radio galaxy Hercules A
caption: The radio galaxy Hercules A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Very Large Array
celestial: Hercules A · constellation Hercules · about z=0.156 (redshift) away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, S. Baum and C. O'Dea (RIT), R. Perley and W. Cotton (NRAO/AUI/NSF), and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: In the center of this image sits a yellowish elliptical galaxy that looks quite ordinary in Hubble's visible-light view. Enormous jets spread out from it, visible only in radio data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in New Mexico. The galaxy is Hercules A, some two billion light-years away.

It is anything but ordinary. The galaxy is roughly a thousand times more massive than the Milky Way and holds a central black hole of about 2.5 billion solar masses. It is also the brightest radio source in the constellation Hercules and one of the brightest outside our galaxy anywhere in the sky.

The jets are beams of very-high-energy plasma, subatomic particles and magnetic fields, fired at nearly the speed of light from near the black hole. They stretch one-and-a-half million light-years, dwarfing the galaxy. Ring-like structures in their outer parts suggest the black hole has erupted several times.

understand.summary: This is a composite of visible light from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and radio data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. The color mapping for each data set is not published.
understand.eye: Radio waves are invisible to the eye, so the jets that dominate this image could never be seen directly, even through a telescope.

explore: The jets' innermost parts cannot be seen because their material moves so fast that its light is beamed away from us. A very hot, X-ray-emitting cloud of gas also surrounds the source but does not appear here. Hubble also shows a companion elliptical galaxy close to the center that may be merging with Hercules A.
